mainTopic: Why a borrower who admits part of a debt must swear, the dispute between רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and the רבנן about a claim made against a son, and the new משנה about witnesses who confirm their signatures but then say the document is invalid.
overview: The amud opens by finishing an explanation from earlier on the daf. A borrower who admits only part of a debt is too embarrassed to deny everything to his lender's face, so the תורה gives him a שבועה to push him to admit the whole debt. This explains the argument between רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and the רבנן about a claim made by the lender's son: would the borrower dare lie to the son? Then a new משנה teaches that witnesses who confirm their own signatures are believed when they add that they were forced, were minors, or were disqualified, unless their handwriting can be proven some other way. רמי בר חמא first limits the second half of that rule. רבא challenges him, because witnesses cannot take back testimony, and ריש לקיש says a signed document counts like testimony already checked in court. So the גמרא moves רמי בר חמא's rule to the first half: a claim of a threat to life is believed, but a claim of money pressure is not, because אין אדם משים עצמו רשע. Finally, a ברייתא shows that רבי מאיר does not believe the witnesses at all. The גמרא starts explaining his reason, and the quote from ריש לקיש continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why the תורה makes a מודה במקצת swear
steps.stepSummary: The borrower really wants to admit the whole debt. He only holds back part of it to buy time until he has money, so the תורה puts a שבועה on him to push him to admit everything.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, he would want to admit the whole debt to him. The reason he did not admit it is so he can dodge him for now. He tells himself: 'Once I have money, I will pay him back.' So the Merciful One said: put an oath on him, so that he will admit the whole thing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes explaining why the תורה says that someone who admits part of a debt (מודה במקצת) must swear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier on the daf, the גמרא said that a borrower will not brazenly deny the whole loan to the lender's face. So when he admits only part, the likely story is that he owes everything and is just stalling for time. The שבועה is meant to pressure him into admitting the full amount.

keyTerms.meaning: One who admits part of a claim against him
To slip away, to dodge (paying for now)
Money (literally, zuz coins)
The Merciful One, meaning the תורה or ה׳
An oath

steps.whyThisMatters: This reason is the key to the argument that comes next. The whole debate depends on whether the borrower is too embarrassed to lie.

phrases.english: And he would want to admit to him all of it.
phrases.notes: He means the borrower is too embarrassed to deny the debt to the lender's face.

phrases.english: And the fact that he did not admit to him
is so that he can dodge him for now,
and he thinks: until I have money
and then I will pay him back.
And the Merciful One said: put an oath on him,
so that he will admit to him all of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the explanation, begun before this section, of why the תורה requires a שבועה from a מודה במקצת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A מודה במקצת swears because he probably owes everything and is only stalling. The שבועה pushes him to admit the full debt.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב: no brazenness even toward the son
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב holds that the borrower will not brazenly lie to the lender's son either. So a partial admission to the son is a normal מודה במקצת, not an honest return of a lost object.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב holds: it makes no difference whether it is the lender himself or his son. The borrower does not act brazenly. Therefore he is not like someone returning a lost object.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now uses the idea from step 1 to explain one side of an argument. The case is someone who admits part of a claim made by the lender's son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the borrower would not dare deny everything to the son either, then admitting part is just stalling, exactly as with the father. So he is a regular מודה במקצת and must swear.

keyTerms.meaning: Acts brazenly, dares to lie to someone's face
One who returns a lost object (an honest person who volunteers information and is exempt from an oath)
It makes no difference

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds:

phrases.aramaic: לָא שְׁנָא בּוֹ וְלָא שְׁנָא בִּבְנוֹ,
phrases.english: it makes no difference whether with him or with his son,
phrases.notes: "Him" is the original lender. "His son" is the lender's son who is now making the claim.

phrases.english: he does not act brazenly,
and therefore he is not one returning a lost object.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the reasoning of step 1 to explain רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's position.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, a borrower is not brazen toward the son either. So a partial admission to the son is not משיב אבידה.

steps.title: The רבנן: brazenness is possible toward the son
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן hold that the borrower would dare lie to the son. Since he chose not to deny everything, his partial admission counts as honestly returning a lost object.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן hold: it is only to the lender himself that he would not act brazenly. To the son, he would. So since he did not act brazenly, he is like someone returning a lost object.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the other side of the argument and explains why the רבנן exempt this borrower.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son never lent the money himself, so the borrower would not be embarrassed to deny everything to him. Since the borrower could easily have denied all of it but still admitted part, he looks honest. He is treated as משיב אבידה and does not swear.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis, the majority opinion
They hold, they are of the opinion
And since he did not

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree on the basic idea from step 1. They argue only about whether a borrower would dare lie to the lender's son. If not, the admission is stalling and he swears (רבי אליעזר בן יעקב). If he would, the admission shows honesty and he is exempt (רבנן).

phrases.english: And the Rabbis hold:
it is with him that he does not act brazenly,
but with his son, he does act brazenly.
And since he did not act brazenly
he is one returning a lost object.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents the opposing view to step 2, completing the explanation of the argument.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the רבנן, a borrower would lie to the son. So choosing to admit part makes him משיב אבידה, and he is exempt from a שבועה.

steps.title: משנה: witnesses who confirm their signature but say it was invalid
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה teaches that witnesses who say 'this is our signature, but we were forced, or were minors, or were disqualified' are believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Witnesses who said: 'This is our handwriting, but we were forced, we were minors, we were disqualified witnesses.' These witnesses are believed.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It deals with witnesses who confirm their signatures on a document but in the same breath say the signing was not valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The document only stands because these witnesses confirm their handwriting. Since we rely on their words to make it valid, we also believe them when they say it is invalid. This is the idea of הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
Our handwriting, our signature
Forced, under pressure
Minors, below the age of being valid witnesses
People disqualified from being witnesses (like relatives)
Believed, trusted

phrases.english: Mishnah: Witnesses who said:
this is our handwriting,
but we were forced,
we were minors, we were disqualified witnesses
they are believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָעֵדִים שֶׁאָמְרוּ: כְּתַב יָדֵינוּ הוּא זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: a new משנה about confirming signatures on documents.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses who confirm their signatures but claim they were forced, underage, or disqualified are believed, and the document is not upheld.

steps.title: משנה: not believed if the handwriting is proven another way
steps.stepSummary: If other witnesses confirm the signatures, or the handwriting can be matched to another document, the original witnesses are not believed when they say it was invalid.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if there are other witnesses that it is their handwriting, or their handwriting shows up on a document from somewhere else, they are not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the other side of the rule. When the document does not depend on the signers' own words, their claim of invalidity is not accepted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the signatures are proven without the signers' help, the document already stands on its own. Now their new claim is simply trying to take back what they signed, and they cannot do that.

keyTerms.meaning: Coming out from another place, a separate document with their handwriting that can be compared
They are not believed

steps.whatToRemember: The witnesses are believed only when the document depends on their own testimony. If their handwriting is proven another way, they cannot cancel the document.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם יֵשׁ עֵדִים שֶׁהוּא כְּתַב יָדָם,
phrases.english: But if there are witnesses that it is their handwriting,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁהָיָה כְּתַב יָדָם יוֹצֵא מִמָּקוֹם אַחֵר
phrases.english: or their handwriting was coming out from another place
phrases.notes: He means another document with their signatures exists, so a court can compare the handwriting.

phrases.english: they are not believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם יֵשׁ עֵדִים שֶׁהוּא כְּתַב יָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the exception to the rule in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the signatures are confirmed independently, the witnesses are not believed when they claim the signing was invalid.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא: the exception applies only to being forced by money
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא says the משנה's 'not believed' rule applies only when they claim they were forced by money. If they say they were forced by a threat to their lives, they are believed even then.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא said: they only taught this where the witnesses said 'we were forced because of money.' But if they said 'we were forced because our lives were threatened,' they are believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with רמי בר חמא, who narrows the second half of the משנה (step 5).
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'we signed falsely because of money pressure' means admitting they did something wrong, and a person cannot make himself a רשע through his own testimony. Signing under a threat to one's life is permitted, so that claim is not self-incriminating. They are believed even when their handwriting is proven another way.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmudic discussion of the משנה
They only taught this rule in the case of
Because of money (pressure involving money)
Because of lives (a threat to their lives)

steps.confusionAlert: רמי בר חמא is not talking about the first case of the משנה, where the witnesses are believed anyway. He is limiting the second case, where their handwriting was proven another way. Even there, a claim of a threat to their lives is believed.

phrases.english: Gemara: Rami bar Chama said:
They taught this only where they said
'we were forced because of money.'
But 'we were forced because of lives'
they are believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the exception taught in step 5 of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's 'not believed' rule applies only to a claim of being forced by money. A claim of being forced by a threat to life is believed even when the signatures are proven another way.

steps.title: רבא: witnesses cannot take back their testimony
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges רמי בר חמא. Once witnesses have testified, they cannot change their story.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: Do they have the power to do that?! Once a witness has testified, he cannot go back and testify differently.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רמי בר חמא's rule from Step 6, which let witnesses cancel a confirmed document by saying they were threatened with death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the signatures are confirmed, the witnesses' testimony already stands. Saying 'we were forced' now is a new testimony that contradicts the first one. There is a rule that a witness cannot contradict his own earlier testimony.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it in his power? He has no right to do this.

keyTerms.term: כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִגִּיד שׁוּב אֵינוֹ חוֹזֵר וּמַגִּיד
keyTerms.meaning: Once he has testified, he cannot go back and testify differently.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
Is it in his power?!
Once he has testified,
he cannot go back and testify again.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רמי בר חמא's rule from Step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: רמי בר חמא's claim that witnesses are believed about a threat to life even after their signatures were confirmed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Witnesses cannot contradict testimony they have already given, so they cannot cancel a confirmed document.

steps.title: A signed document counts like testimony given in court
steps.stepSummary: רבא blocks a possible defense. One might say the 'no going back' rule only covers spoken testimony, but ריש לקיש says signed witnesses are like witnesses already questioned in court.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say this rule only applies to spoken testimony, but not to a document, didn't ריש לקיש say: witnesses signed on a document are treated like witnesses whose testimony was already examined in court!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers a defense before anyone can raise it. He shows that the 'no going back' rule applies to written documents too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone could argue that a signature is weaker than speaking in court, so it can be taken back. ריש לקיש's rule closes that gap: a signature already has the full status of testimony checked in בית דין. So רמי בר חמא's rule, as stated in Step 6, cannot stand.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say. Introduces a possible defense.
Spoken, out loud.
Their testimony was examined in court.

phrases.english: And if you will say:
this applies only to spoken testimony,
but with a document, no,
but didn't Reish Lakish say:
witnesses signed on a document

phrases.aramaic: נַעֲשָׂה כְּמִי שֶׁנֶּחְקְרָה עֵדוּתָן בְּבֵית דִּין!
phrases.english: are treated like those whose testimony was examined in court!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: הָנֵי מִילֵּי עַל פֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens רבא's challenge by blocking the escape that documents are different.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible defense that the rule only covers spoken testimony.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ריש לקיש gives signed witnesses the same status as witnesses examined in court, so they cannot go back on it either.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא's rule moved to the first clause
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves רמי בר חמא's rule to the case where the witnesses alone are believed. They are believed if they claim a threat to life, but not if they claim a threat to money, because a person cannot make himself wicked.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the statement was said about the first clause, 'these are believed.' רמי בר חמא said: This was taught only when they said 'we were forced by a threat to our lives.' But if they said 'we were forced by money,' they are not believed. Why? A person cannot make himself wicked.
steps.whatsHappening: Because of רבא's challenge, the גמרא changes where רמי בר חמא's rule belongs. It now applies only to the first clause of the משנה, where nobody else confirmed the signatures.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first clause, the witnesses are believed because they are the only reason we know about the signatures at all. רמי בר חמא now limits that: signing under threat of death is not a sin, so they can say it. Signing falsely to avoid losing money is a sin, and בית דין does not accept a person's testimony that makes himself a רשע.

keyTerms.meaning: It was said about the first clause.
Because of a threat to life.
Because of a threat to money.
A person cannot make himself wicked. His testimony against himself is not accepted.

steps.confusionAlert: This version flips Step 6. Before, a threat to life helped the witnesses even after their signatures were confirmed. Now the rule is only about the first clause, where nobody else confirmed the signatures. There, a threat to life is believed, but a threat to money is not.
steps.whatToRemember: Final version of רמי בר חמא: when nobody else confirms the signatures, the witnesses are believed if they say 'forced by a threat to life,' but not if they say 'forced by money,' because אין אדם משים עצמו רשע.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule אין אדם משים עצמו רשע shows up all over the laws of testimony. Here it explains why a witness who claims a money threat loses even the trust the משנה gave him.

phrases.english: Rather, when it was stated,
it was stated about the first clause:
phrases.notes: The first clause is the case where nobody else confirms the signatures (Step 4).

phrases.english: "these are believed."
Rami bar Chama said:
They taught this only when they said:
"We were forced because of a threat to our lives,"
but if they said:
"We were forced because of money,"
they are not believed.
What is the reason?
A person cannot make himself wicked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's challenge by moving the rule to a different part of the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moving the statement to a different clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רמי בר חמא was talking about the second clause, where the signatures were confirmed by others.
steps.terutzMaskana: רמי בר חמא was talking about the first clause, and he sets a limit there: a threat to life is believed, a threat to money is not.

steps.title: רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue about witnesses cancelling their document
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: רבי מאיר says the witnesses are not believed to cancel the document, and the חכמים say they are believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: They are not believed to make it invalid. These are the words of רבי מאיר. The חכמים say: They are believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא. It shows that the משנה's rule, that the witnesses alone are believed, is actually a dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה follows the חכמים, who believe the witnesses. רבי מאיר disagrees: even when nobody else confirms the signatures, the witnesses cannot cancel the document.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught. Introduces a ברייתא.
To make it invalid.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
They are not believed to make it invalid,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
And the Sages say: They are believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: a ברייתא with a dispute about the משנה's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: the witnesses are not believed to cancel their document. חכמים: they are believed.

steps.title: What is רבי מאיר's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים's reason is clear: the same mouth that made the document valid can make it invalid. The גמרא asks what רבי מאיר's reason is.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for the רבנן, based on their reason: the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted. But for רבי מאיר, what is his reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says it understands the חכמים, and asks why רבי מאיר would not believe the witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the witnesses' own words, we would not know the document is valid. So their words can also limit it: הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר. רבי מאיר seems to ignore this strong logic, so the גמרא asks for his reason.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense for... Sets up a contrast with 'but for X.'
The mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted. The same words that create something can also limit it.

phrases.english: It makes sense for the Sages,
based on their reason,
that the mouth that forbade
phrases.notes: Here "forbade" means the witnesses made the document valid, so it binds the borrower.

phrases.english: is the mouth that permitted.
But for Rabbi Meir, what is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the חכמים's reasoning (הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר) and asks only for רבי מאיר's reason.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי מאיר does not believe the witnesses, even though their own words are what make the document valid.

steps.title: Explaining רבי מאיר for disqualified witnesses and minors
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains רבי מאיר for two of the claims. The lender checks that his witnesses are kosher, and for minors it starts to bring ריש לקיש's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for disqualified witnesses, because the lender himself checks carefully from the start and only then has them sign. Minors too, as רבי שמעון בן לקיש said. For ריש לקיש said:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins answering for רבי מאיר, one claim at a time. It ends by setting up a quote from ריש לקיש that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A lender would never let disqualified witnesses sign his own document, so their claim of being פסולים is not believable. For minors, the explanation will come from ריש לקיש's rule. The wording 'it makes sense for these' hints that the גמרא will then ask about the claim 'we were forced.'

keyTerms.meaning: People who are not allowed to be witnesses.
Checks very carefully.
Minors, children under the age of being a witness.

phrases.english: It makes sense for disqualified witnesses,
the lender himself, from the start,
checks carefully and has them sign.
Minors too,
as Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said.
For Reish Lakish said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering Step 11's question about רבי מאיר, one claim at a time.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Disqualified witnesses: the lender checks them before they sign. Minors: explained by ריש לקיש's rule, which is quoted next.
